the ask is 'go the distance to the right of the point in both parts', i.e. carry both parts to a common accuracy, and 530ef987f8 (2008-02-03, 'print complex numbers to a combined precision for both parts') did exactly that on the 1.1 branch -- the release the file asks for it by. It is still the scalar rule: format(...,CC) at gmp1.d:246 derives one accuracy from exponent(z), the larger part, so at printingPrecision 6 a real part more than six decimal places below the imaginary one falls below the printed resolution and 1e-30+ii prints as ii. Matrix and vector entries reach expression CC (reals.m2:494) instead and format the parts independently, so they show | 1e-30+ii |. That difference is not a defect: showing a different number of digits for a CC and for the entry of a matrix over CC is the expected consequence of the two rules, and the scalar rule is the considered one -- a part thirty orders below the other is not part of a six-significant-digit rendering of the number. Note the file's own transcript shows the PRE-530ef987f8 independent formatting, which today's scalar path cannot produce at any printingAccuracy=-1 setting, so the file illustrates one convention while its sentence asks for the other; both halves now show both parts under their own rule

1/3 == 1./3 is still false, and it is the right answer. The comparison is exact, not a promotion: compare(x:RR, y:QQ) is mpfr_cmp_q (gmp.d:1475-1479), which compares the double against the rational without rounding either, and since the nearest double to 1/3 is below 1/3 the result is 1/3 > 1./3, which M2 reports. Dan's proposed fix, making them compare equal, would require rounding the rational to the float's precision first -- that is what would make == inexact, and it would break transitivity against nearby rationals. Where the float is exact the two do agree: 1/2 == 0.5 and 1/4 == .25 are both true, which is the tell that promotion is not what is happening. mpfr_cmp_q predates the file (510344c38c, 2008-01), so nothing changed here and the answer to the file's closing question, 'Is it okay?', was settled by leaving it alone

done, by the autoconf idiom rather than by version arithmetic: where a particular version is needed, configure either checks the version or checks for the feature that version brought, and the second is the normal case. configure.ac carries 107 feature-test invocations -- 34 AC_SEARCH_LIBS, 34 AC_CHECK_HEADER, 14 AC_COMPILE_IFELSE, 11 AC_LINK_IFELSE, 10 AC_CHECK_HEADERS, 7 AC_RUN_IFELSE and so on -- including compile-and-link probes against flint, givaro, gmp and libnormaliz headers, which is exactly 'checking that recent versions appear' expressed as what the code needs rather than as a number. Explicit version gates exist for the two cases where no feature test would do: GNU make 3.81 is rejected at :209, and Arb errors 'found but too old' at :902. Separately, anything M2 builds itself is version-exact -- 27 of 37 libraries/*/Makefile.in pin a VERSION with a SHA256SUM. Recorded first as open on a count of version comparisons, which was the wrong measurement: a low count of those is what a well-written configure script looks like, not evidence of a gap

a non-goal rather than a gap, and the ecosystem settled it the other way. getWWW is a hand-rolled HTTP/1.1 client from 1996 (http.m2, Copyright 1996) that writes request lines onto a socket with four headers, and delegates HTTPS to a subprocess -- 'openssl s_client -quiet -verify 1' at http.m2:45-48. It is a plain method() with no options, so there is nowhere to pass a cookie, and nothing reads Set-Cookie. But no consumer wants one: OnlineLookup does stateless query-string GETs against oeis.org/search and wayback.cecm.sfu.ca/cgi-bin/isc/lookup, and ReflexivePolytopesDB the same against quark.itp.tuwien.ac.at/cgi-bin/cy/cydata.cgi. That package also shows what happened instead: it carries a documented Access option taking 'm2', 'curl' or 'wget' (ReflexivePolytopesDB.m2:93-98), so an author who hit getWWW's limits shelled out rather than asking for the feature -- and curl brings cookies, redirects, TLS, proxies and auth together, each of which getWWW would otherwise reimplement, cookies being the first of the sequence rather than the last. The second ask, 'also the email address option!', is two words that cannot be reconstructed from the file; the likeliest reading is a From: header, but nothing in the tree corroborates it and guessing was not worth publishing. Would be worth revisiting only for a concrete endpoint someone wants that requires a cookie

reproduces, and it is not merely counter-intuitive as the file says -- it contradicts the documentation. ov_debugging.m2:102-107 promises that after typing end, 'the debugger will be entered again ... at the point inside the function g from which the function f was called', and that listLocalSymbols will then show g's local variables. a design musing that was never taken up, and the file knows it -- it ends 'Feedback on that idea would be welcome'. The description still holds: degree of the zero ring element is -infinity, while a zero vector keeps the degree of whatever it came from, so degree(0*F_1) is {0}. The proposal was to make R seriously graded with distinct zero elements of each degree, and the file itself names the reason nobody did: you would then have to decide whether r == s and r === s agree for zeros of different degrees, which is a change to equality semantics across the whole system for a cosmetic gain. Fifteen years on there is one zero per ring and no sign anyone wants otherwise

done, and my first reading was wrong. I checked class degreeLift, found an unbound Symbol, and recorded the ask unmet -- but the feature is not a global function of that name, it is a derivation inside map. ringmap.m2:97-104 builds degmapmatrix from the DegreeMap and, when the user supplies no DegreeLift, derives one by solving quotientRemainder against it, raising 'degreeLift: degree not liftable' where no lift exists; identity is short-circuited. Verified: for map(A,B,gens A,DegreeMap => reverse) the cache holds a DegreeLift FunctionClosure at ringmap.m2:101 which sends {1,0} to {0,1}, correctly inverting reverse, and a map with no DegreeMap gets identity. So 'we can compute the degreeLift function for the user automatically' is exactly what map now does. #2580, DegreeLift not preserving homogeneity for multigraded maps, still reproduces and is a separate live bug in the same mechanism

the same puzzle as #1477, 'Dispatching of lift and promote', which asks why lift's method is installed the way it is, observes that Ring is not among RingElement's ancestors so the dispatch is hard to account for, and concludes 'the documentation is rather thin in this area'. reproduces cold and the order matters: X11 .. a errors in a fresh session and only works once vars(-11) has memoized into varIndices, so running the file's two lines in reverse reads as fixed. varName (indeterminates.m2:8-13) defines the whole scheme -- X<n> for negative indices, x<n> for indices at least 52 -- but reverseVars (:24-33) inverts only single letters, match("^[a-zA-Z]$",s) at :28, plus whatever a prior vars ZZ call registered. reproduces byte for byte and the cause is one line. net Superscript (expressions.m2:774-779) raises the exponent by 1 + depth n, computed from the exponent's own net, so the offset ignores how tall the base is; the parenthesized quotient ring measures (height, depth) = (3,3), six lines with its baseline in the middle, and the exponent lands on row 2 of 6 exactly as the file's arrow marks. Raising by max(1 + depth n, height b) against the base net puts it above the top line, which is what the file asks for, and is byte-identical to today for a one-line base and for a matrix base -- checked, since the tempting height b - 1 breaks the ordinary case by dropping the exponent onto the baseline. Not a deliberate choice: git log -S 'n^(1+depth n)' returns only 647f7532b3, Initial revision. #3198 is about the parser's precedence for _ and ^, not where a superscript is drawn

unmet on all three counts and data is genuinely lost, measured rather than read: after zzf << "hello"; zzf = null and two collectGarbage() calls the file is empty and openFiles() still lists it. At normal exit it does reach disk, via closem (d/stdio.d:575-583) registered with atend -- which flushes but does not close. Two blockers, and the second is the interesting one. There is no finalizer on the file type (git grep -i finaliz over d/stdio0.d d/stdio.d d/stdiop.d exits 1; every GC_REGISTER_FINALIZER in the tree is for foreign pointers, mysql, pthreads or engine objects). And openfiles (d/stdio.d:154-158) is a strong-reference list that addfile pushes every file onto and only rmfile removes, from cleanUp, after close -- so an unclosed file is reachable from a GC root and can never be collected, which is what openFiles() still listing it demonstrates. The two halves of the file are in tension: the flush-at-exit net that makes the common case work depends on that same pinning. #1515 is a hard second blocker, registerFinalizer broken since <=1.12 with #2728 on the same GC warnings and #1852 closed as its duplicate

Filing that one; Schubert2 calls the CoefficientRing form at five sites. (2) is met, and Dan's own '(or does it?)' is answered: degrees and degreeLength are preserved variable by variable (a {{1,0}}/{{0,1}} tower flattens to degrees {{0,1,0,0},{0,0,1,0}}, degreeLength 4 to 4) and homogeneity survives the map, by the 2008 degree-joining series 0126f8f60b..3f8ebb6ab1 plus 1da8ef003c and bf728fe883; matrix2.m2:181 now relies on it. (3) is verbatim still true -- degreeLength is never reduced and the order is the product order (monoids.m2:681-682) -- and its live symptom is #3887, whose reporter works around it with newRing(..., MonomialOrder => GRevLex, Degrees => {1,1}); commented there. A doc gap found on the way: flattenRing-doc.m2 has zero mentions of degrees, homogeneity or monomial order, which is what #651 should absorb

both halves unmet, and the second is measurable without the first. Applying a ring map never short-circuits: ringmap.m2 contains no raw-ring comparison and RingMap RingElement (:169-175) always calls rawRingMapEval, so map(zzB,zzB) -- which satisfies zzid == 1, source === target and zzid === id_zzB, since ringmap.m2:31 computes exactly that predicate for comparison -- still costs 2.55ms per application on a 210-term polynomial and returns its argument. The first half is real but small: for a tower flattenRing builds a fresh raw ring rather than reusing R.FlatMonoid (raw zzS =!= raw zzR, zzR.FlatMonoid =!= monoid zzS) even though describe of the two monoids is character-identical, but caching from b25a44b6d1 (2008-10-24) already amortizes it -- 4.0ms on the first call for a 16-variable tower, 4.1us after. filed as one issue covering the whole for-bounds gap, with 1-for-sequence-idea and 1-for-by as duplicates of it. Bart Snapp's example still fails: for i from (0,0) to (5,6) gives 'expected an integer' while the form the file compares it to, for j in (0,0)..(5,6), iterates all nine pairs -- verified. evalForCode (d/evaluate.d:314) is the whole story. The in clause accepts a Sequence, a List, or any iterable through getIterator and getNextFunction (:331-341); the from and to clauses accept only a ZZcell passing isInt (:348-358), because j and n are C ints. And there is no step at all: forCode (d/parse.d:252) has inClause, fromClause, toClause, whenClause, listClause and doClause and no field for one, and "by" appears nowhere in the d sources as a keyword -- which is why 1-for-by's first example fails as 'no method for adjacent objects: 0 (of class ZZ) SPACE by (of class Symbol)' rather than as a for-loop error. So the loop body already handles what the bounds refuse, and both needs are reachable today through the in clause: for i in reverse(0..4) descends, for i in select(0..10, zzk -> zzk%2==0) steps, both verified. Filed on the same basis as #4557 and #4563, convenience over a working spelling. the two resource-limit steps shipped and the security content is better done from outside the process. Of the seven-step recipe, step 1 is limitFiles and step 6 is limitProcesses (d/system.d:204-221, documented ov_system.m2:2044-2062), both from 778e7f0cad (2012-03-13) -- the same commit as the --read-only-files the file itself credits, which still works: openOut under it is blocked. Steps 2-5, the privilege separation, are absent; there is no chroot or setuid anywhere in d/, c/ or e/, and class sandbox is Symbol. Two reasons not to pursue it. The recipe is fork-then-drop-privileges and fork's own documentation now says very few operations can be safely done in the child of a multithreaded program, even allocating memory -- M2 became multithreaded after this was written. And sandboxing the whole M2 process externally is strictly better than building privilege separation in: a container runtime, systemd unit confinement, a seccomp or firejail-style wrapper or a VM all cover the engine and every library M2 links, do not depend on M2 being correct about it, and need no fork inside a threaded process. Macaulay2Web is one consumer that does exactly that, out of tree. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply. One live gap that is not this file's ask: --read-only-files is documented nowhere in Macaulay2Doc or the man page, unlike limitFiles and limitProcesses. #519 is the adjacent resource-limits issue

works now, and correctly for the case that can be correct. frac(QQ[x]/x^2[y]) returns a FractionField instead of 'not implemented yet: fraction fields of polynomial rings over rings other than ZZ, QQ, or a finite field', because 711507e071 (pzinn, 2024-02-27, PR #3177 'frac of iterated ring') made factoryAlmostGood recurse through the whole chain (enginering.m2:335-342) where it previously looked only one level down at coefficientRing and so refused iterated rings wholesale. The guard at enginering.m2:350 is still there; it was widened, not removed. For a domain base it is sound: over frac((QQ[a]/(a^2-2))[y]), a^2 == 2, y*(1/y) == 1, 1/a*a == 1 and (y+a)/(y+a) == 1. Found while checking this, and NOT filed here because it is the live core of bugs/mike/0-frac-bug, still todo: the same guard never asks whether any quotient in the chain is prime, so frac accepts non-domains and builds a ring that is not one. frac's own documentation says the input is an integral domain. In frac(ZZ[t]/(t^4)) -- 0-frac-bug's ring -- t =!= 0, t^4 == 0, t*(1/t) == 1 and yet (t^4)*(1/t) == 0 while t^3*(t*(1/t)) == t^3, so the same product grouped two ways gives 0 and t^3. That file's own transcript is fixed, its product l now being 1 rather than a nilpotent denominator, so it could have been settled fixed on the symptom Filed as #4576 and bugs/mike/0-frac-bug settled as its duplicate.

unmet, and the answer is cheaper than the file imagined -- reframed onto FLINT, since PARI left the tree in e79bd82855 (2025-03-07). findGalois (galois.m2:95-121) asks a hook, the only hook is ConwayPolynomials, and its data is FLINT's Conway table (ConwayPolynomials.m2:13, 'the data comes libflint', via a2fd44e9f0). Outside that table it falls to galois.m2:113, a brute-force search over dense random monic polynomials, then findPrimitive. Measured: conwayPolynomial(3,100) is null, GF(3,100) takes 6.5s then 4.8s and yields a 67-term modulus that differs on every call, while rawConwayPolynomial(3,100,true) -- FLINT's fq_nmod_ctx_init -- returns a modulus with 3 nonzero coefficients in 2.2ms. ConwayPolynomials.m2:16 hard-codes false, so GF never sees it. GF(3,582), the pari thread's own example, does not finish at all in any practical sense: left running without a timeout it was still going after 55 minutes at 99 percent of a core and 261MB, and was killed rather than completing. Two aggravating details: the modulus is non-deterministic, so GF(3,100) in two sessions gives incompatible fields, and findPrimitive (galois.m2:118) is computed then discarded on the FlintBig path (galois.m2:174-181), i.e. wasted precisely in the slow cases. Coupled cost for whoever takes it: a non-Conway modulus makes map(GaloisField,GaloisField) error by design (ConwayPolynomials.m2:42), which is #2143. #1917 is adjacent, same galois.m2 block

unmet, and instead of declining it gcd returns a common divisor that is not greatest. Over QQ[a]/(a^2-1), which is QQ x QQ, with e = (1+a)/2 and f = (1-a)/2 verified idempotent and orthogonal: for F = e*(x-1)+f*(x-2) and G = e*(x-1)+f*(x-3), d = e*(x-1)+f has degree 1 and divides both, yet gcd(F,G) is 1. My first example, (x^2-1)*(x-a) against (x^2-1)*(x+a), gave the right answer x^2-1 and was a coincidence -- both components share a gcd there. Cause identified and the capability already exists: gcd calls the two-argument rawGCD (factor.m2:26-28) with no minimal polynomial, so an extension in the coefficient ring is invisible and only the base-field part comes back. Over K = QQ[a]/(a^6-a^3-1) with R = K[t], F = t^6-t^3-1 and G = (t-a)*(t+a), t-a divides both and the front end says 1, while rawGCD(raw F, raw G, raw (ideal K)_0) returns t-a. That is Mike's 2009 diagnosis verbatim, bugs/mike/0-gcd-doc.m2 line 3, 'rawGCDRingElement is not being called from the front end'. Also: the guard Dan proposed in #321 -- 'just give an error if the ring is a quotient ring' -- exists at factor.m2:24 but tests only the top ring, so gcd errors in QQ[a]/(a^2-1) and proceeds in (QQ[a]/(a^2-1))[x], and likewise for pzinn's own ZZ[y]/(y^2+3) example. Third guard-depth defect of this cohort after #4576 and #4578. bugs/mike/0-gcd-doc.m2 is left todo on purpose: it is a 120-line multi-ask file covering factor over toField ('NOT CORRECT!!'), bivariate gcd and missing documentation, so it must be read against this issue rather than settled as its duplicate. #1958 is the units-in-a-field case Mike called expected

met, in a better place than the file asked for. There is no such check in configure.ac -- every gmp test there is presence or version, including the only AC_RUN_IFELSE at :918-940, which is a compile-time __GNU_MP_VERSION predicate. But tests/normal/random.m2 is exactly this test: its first line is '-- let's make sure the random number generator doesn't change', and it pins the output of random 100 and of five seed settings against hard-coded vectors, with the superseded pre-1.1 vectors left in comments as the record of the last change. It runs in both build systems and therefore in CI, and it passes today against gmp 6.3.0 -- verified by loading it under --no-randomize, which is how the harness runs tests and which the file's own lines 3-5 explain. M2 does depend on gmp here: random ZZ reaches mpz_urandomm on a gmp_randinit_default state (e/interface/random.cpp:25,63), and gmp documents that default as free to change between releases. A configure probe would be strictly worse -- it cannot see M2's own seeding layer and would fire on machines that only consume prebuilt packages. Residue not filed: random QQ and random RR (random.cpp:182-183, :217, :245, the latter via mpfr_urandomb) have no pinned vectors

decided by the file's own author, twice. 511504951f (2009-03-27, eight days after the file) implemented exactly this -- 'change caching of example outputs so the hash code is not dependent on the type List', switching the stored value to toSequence -- and 7c41af8e0e (2009-10-06) reverted it, 'change stored example inputs back to a list, instead of a sequence / be prepared to fix the resulting problems', leaving a standing instruction that survives verbatim at examples.m2:165-166: 'don't convert "ex" on the next line to a sequence, because the hash code for caching example outputs will change'. the cited idea does not apply to M2's design, and the measurable headroom is negligible. Brent's paper is about shortening probe sequences in open-addressed scatter storage; M2 uses separate chaining -- KeyValuePair is {key, hash, value, next} at d/parse.d:463 -- and hashtables.dd:137-142 records that new entries are prepended deliberately, because appending 'might cause a reader to encounter the same key twice' for readers that do not lock the table. Adopting open addressing would mean discarding that lock-free-reader invariant. Measured over 10^6 operations against a 0.372s interpreter floor: MutableHashTable store 0.723s and lookup 0.660s against MutableList 0.342s and 0.451s, so a hash lookup is about 1.5x an array index end to end and is dominated by interpreter dispatch rather than probing; a collision-free table could save tens of nanoseconds per operation. No issue among 4600+ has ever reported hash-table speed, the paper's URL in the file is a mangled Google redirect that no longer resolves, and the note names no symptom, benchmark or threshold. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply. #2591 was about hash-code quality rather than table structure

duplicate of #1608, where Dan restated this ask himself in 2020 with the rationale the one-line file lacks: 'much more useful ... would be to implement red-black trees, which are a type of height balanced trees, where the keys can be any objects of Macaulay2 for which ? provides a total ordering'. Commented there rather than filed, because the comment's contribution is that the premise fails three ways, measured: ? is partial (1 ? "a", symbol x ? 1 and {1} ? (1,) all give 'no method'), it can answer 'incomparable' for Sets rather than one of < = >, and #650 still reproduces so it is unstable where it does answer -- sort applied twice to a list of Sets alternates between two orders. So a balanced-tree type cannot take 'any objects for which ? is a total order' as its key domain; it needs a comparison supplied at construction, or a documented restriction, or #650 fixed first. Current state for the record: Core has no ordered container at all, and no distributed package implements one

the premise is measurably false. One help call costs nothing: M2 -q -e 'help merge' peaks at 125148KB against a 125312KB do-nothing baseline, i.e. inside run-to-run noise; 200 help nodes cost +3MB; and about("merge", Body => true), which opens every installed database and reads every value, costs +7MB. There is no 'whole help is read in' event, because documentation lives in per-package databases opened on demand and memoized (system.m2:352-354) and retrieved one key at a time, with the value only evaluated at that moment (document.m2:379-381). The debug-mode limit the email is about still exists and was doubled for debug builds in 230286b1f5 (2021-06-26): run.m2:114-116 sets GC_MAXIMUM_HEAP_SIZE=800M when --enable-debug appears in the configure arguments and 400M otherwise, and Dan's own follow-up 76361ca44c (2011-02-19) raised the example limits five months after this file. Two things unverified: the 800M branch, since neither M2 available here is an --enable-debug build, and whether ulimit -m at run.m2:13 is the no-op on Linux that RLIMIT_RSS semantics suggest. #1879 is a different phenomenon, bdwgc heap fragmentation during html generation on i386

no leak, measured rather than inspected. Dan answered his own question the same day he asked it. The file is his 2008-12-10 email -- 'For a projective variety hilbertFunction() simply applies itself to the underlying graded ring. Similarly for coherent sheaves. This might be unexpected behavior. Should we fix it?' -- with Eisenbud's reply 27 minutes later saying the right answer for a sheaf is the Hilbert function of the global section module, via Hom(mm^d, M) with d from the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity, and asking 'Worth including automatically?'. 8b32397e67, committed that same day, is 'disable hilbertFunction etc. on projective varieties': the method ae25d821e5 had added in 2000 (hilbertFunction(ZZ,CoherentSheaf) delegating to F.module) gained a notImplemented() guard, and 2964a771ad (2021-11-23) removed it altogether. Today hilbertFunction has nine methods, none for CoherentSheaf or ProjectiveVariety, and both error with 'no method found'. Eisenbud's global-sections capability was never added. hilbertPolynomial still delegates the naive way for both (Varieties.m2:198 and :361), which the file itself calls okay and which CoherentSheaf equality depends on at :376. The file's other pointer is stale: only one 'temporarily disabled' remains in the tree, at help.m2:305, and it is about broken links

reproduces byte for byte: with A = QQ[a], B = QQ[b] and C = A**B, substitute(vars A, C) gives isHomogeneous false and degrees {{{0,0}},{{0,0}}} while degrees C is {{1,0},{0,1}}. The file's own framing is right -- 'if only substitute would pay attention to how C was constructed from A' -- and the information is derivable: map(C,A) carries no DegreeMap, and supplying the obvious one, map(C, A, {C_0}, DegreeMap => d -> d | {0}), makes it homogeneous with degrees {{{0,0}},{{1,0}}}. The tensor already computes it. monoids.m2:692 applies d -> join(d,N0) to the first factor's degrees inline and :694 stores only the second factor's map as opts.DegreeMap. I predicted from that asymmetry that substitute(vars B, C) would work where vars A fails; it does not, both are non-homogeneous with zero degrees, so the stored map is not consulted either and the fix is to plumb it rather than to add the missing half. Second row of this session where the needed information exists and the front end does not use it, after #4583's minimal polynomial. #2905 is the adjacent tensor-and-degrees bug that three settled rows already point at

the collision the file describes cannot happen, guarded three ways. The generated header is include/M2/config.h (configure.ac:4), not include/config.h, and every M2 site includes it namespaced -- d/types.h:1 and e/engine-includes.hpp:10 use <M2/config.h>, c/scc.h:3 uses "M2/config.h" -- so CPPFLAGS=-I/tmp/foo with /tmp/foo/config.h cannot shadow it; the builder would have to create /tmp/foo/M2/config.h deliberately. Even then there is a sentinel: configure.ac:524 defines M2_CONFIG_H with the comment 'a macro definition to ensure our config.h was the one loaded' and d/types.h:2-3 raises #error without it. And the flag order the file asks for is in place: config.Makefile.in:70-74 prepends -I@abs_top_srcdir@/include, -I@abs_top_builddir@/include and -I$(BUILTLIBPATH)/include ahead of the builder's $(CPPFLAGS), with d/Makefile.in:170 carrying the comment "it's important that *our* directories get searched first". d/ and e/ do differ, but in M2_CPPFLAGS placement, which holds only -D flags -- last in d/Makefile.in:171 and first in e/Makefile.common.in:4 -- so a builder passing -UNDEBUG would be overridden in one and win in the other. That is a separate, small inconsistency with a clean closing condition, recorded rather than filed. Residual hole outside the file's scope: make CPPFLAGS=... on the command line still clobbers the chain, which config.Makefile.in:58-60 acknowledges

it does something definite now: it errors. R = QQ[u,u] then R_"u" gives 'variable not found in ring' rather than the random generator the file reports, and it errors consistently across repeated calls. String indexing itself is unharmed -- on a ring with distinct names S_"v" returns v, and a name that is absent errors the same way. So the ask, 'it should do something more definite', is met. One wrinkle worth noting for whoever touches the message: for QQ[u,u] the name is not absent but ambiguous, so 'variable not found in ring' describes the situation imprecisely even though refusing is right

the need is served and the change would cost more than it buys. InfiniteNumber is still a type and class infinity is still InfiniteNumber, so the ask is unmet -- but the bridge it asks for exists: numeric infinity returns an RR, and numeric_100 infinity honours a precision, so 'an infinite real of the current defaultPrecision' is available on demand. What the file proposes beyond that is abolishing the symbolic class, and that class is load-bearing as a sentinel: options res carries LengthLimit => infinity, SyzygyLimit => infinity and PairLimit => infinity, compared against integers, and #3656 uses infinity the same way. Collapsing it into an RR would change what those comparisons mean across the tree. The friction the proposal would remove is real and tracked -- #1597, open since 2020, still reproduces exactly: infinity * 0_RR is 0 while (1/0_RR) * 0_RR is NotANumber and infinity * 0_R errors outright -- but that issue asks for consistency rather than unification. A judgment, so overrule it cheaply

the investigation the file asks for has a definite answer, and it is yes. dpkg handles it structurally rather than per package: install-info declares 'interest-noawait /usr/share/info' as a file trigger, /usr/share/info/dir is owned by no package and maintained by that trigger, and macaulay2-common needs no .triggers file of its own -- dpkg fires install-info's whenever any package adds or removes files there. The entries are present here, /usr/share/info/dir carrying 24 Macaulay2 lines including '* Macaulay2Doc: (Macaulay2Doc). Macaulay2 documentation', and the packages ship one .info.gz per distributed package. So removing the package does remove the dir entries, with no maintainer-script machinery -- which is why macaulay2.postinst contains no install-info call. The concern was real when written: dpkg triggers were new in the 2007-2008 era and before them packages ran install-info from postinst and prerm themselves. Checked against the Ubuntu PPA build of the Debian source package rather than Debian unstable

the file defers itself and the idiom would not help. Its first line is 'defer this:', its body an observation that texinfo menu items can point at a line within a node, and its last 'Maybe we can use it.' -- no problem statement, no reproducer, no acceptance criterion, and nothing in the issue tracker has ever mentioned it. M2 uses none of it: format.m2:322-328 is the only menu generator and emits '* key::' or '* key: node.', node granularity by construction, with byte offsets recorded per node at installPackage.m2:402 for the tag table alone. Nor would it pay: the form solves intra-node navigation for long prose nodes, as in the Emacs manual where one node documents dozens of hooks, whereas M2 documents one node per symbol -- 2010 nodes in a megabyte, typically 50 to 120 lines. getWWW is interruptible in both phases, tested in a pty with a real ^C. Blocked in connect to 192.0.2.1, an RFC 5737 address that black-holes: ^C returns to the prompt about 4 seconds in with 'error: can't open socket : Interrupted system call', where the connect itself would run some 130 seconds. Blocked reading from a local server that accepts and never answers: ^C gives 'error: interrupted', the prompt returns and 1+1 evaluates. So the transcript in the file -- two ^C's, then the Exit (y/n) prompt and an abnormal exit -- no longer happens. The commented-out SETJMP(interrupt_jump) block at scclib.c:760-765 is still present and still marked FIXME, but it is not what makes this work: SIGINT arrives without SA_RESTART, connect returns EINTR, and the flag check surfaces it. #145, 'getWWW should time out', is open and asks for a different thing, a bound for when nobody is there to interrupt

the guess is right and the saving is worth having. Every List construction folds the whole list: basic.d:114-117 does r.hash = hash(r), and hash(x:List) at :82-85 is the element-by-element fold with multiplier 1299833 over the seed x.Class.hash + 23407. Cost measured: join of two 200k lists takes 11.2ms, while the identical fold over the resulting 400k elements takes 7.5-8.5ms -- measurable because a Sequence's hash is not cached, basic.d:33-36 refolding on every call -- against 0.69us to read a List's stored hash. So roughly two-thirds of join is hashing. And the fold is combinable: h(L++M) = 1299833^(#M) * (hash L - c) + hash M mod 2^64 with c = hash class L + 23407, verified on seven cases including both empty sides, mixed element types and nested lists. both silent cases confirmed, and the asymmetry looks deliberate rather than missed. unmet, and low priority -- IPv6 transport works everywhere, only the literal spelling is missing. Measured against a server bound to [::1]:24602: openInOut "$ip6-localhost:24602" opens, SCSCP newConnection("ip6-localhost",24602) connects far enough to reach the handshake, getWWW "http://ip6-localhost:24602/" returns HTTP/1.0 200 OK -- and the literal form of all three errors. the mismatch is gone. The error was that poincare Ideal computed the series of the quotient -- 'poincare ((ring I)^1/I)' -- while module Ideal copied I.cache.poincare onto image generators I, the submodule, whose series is different. Today poincare Ideal := I -> poincare comodule I (hilbert.m2:81) with comodule Ideal := I -> cokernel generators I (matrix1.m2:438), and module Ideal := (cacheValue symbol module)(I -> image generators I) (matrix1.m2:440) has the poincare-copying line deleted. Measured over QQ[x,y] with I = ideal(x^2,x*y): poincare I is 1-2*T^2+T^3, poincare module I is 2*T^2-T^3, and they sum to 1 as they must; module I does not inherit the ideal's value. Checked the MonomialIdeal path too, since poincare MonomialIdeal does cache under I.cache.poincare (monideal.m2:131): for monomialIdeal(x^2,x*y) that value is 1-2*T^2+T^3, the quotient's series, and module J still comes back with no cached poincare -- so there is nothing left to copy onto the wrong module

unmet as asked, and not worth the cost: the checks would run uname and a directory test in every login shell to defend against a shared home directory spanning architectures, which is Dan's 2006 scenario (his transcript checks uname -m/-s/-r/-p on rhodium) and is rare now. setup() is otherwise unchanged in shape: it writes ~/.profile-Macaulay2 and inserts a loader into ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile or ~/.zprofile (files.m2:499-508), hard-coding the prefix into PATH, MANPATH, INFOPATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH (:439-443), and the bash template's only logic is avoiding a duplicate entry (:410-418) -- nothing tests that the directory still exists or which machine it is on. maintainer's call: a pruned ring is a different ring, and giving the eliminated symbols values in it -- even optionally -- trades a clear error for cross-ring confusion of the kind #666 and 0-synonyms-and-collisions are about. Unmet as asked, and the state is worth recording. use assigns only gens Rp, so for R = QQ[a,b,c]/(a-b-1) and Rp = minimalPresentation R = QQ[b..c], after use Rp we have ring a = R and ring b = Rp, and both a+b and a*b error. The ingredient the ask needs does exist: R.minimalPresentationMap is map(Rp,R,{b+1,b,c}), sending a to b+1 in Rp, so an implementation would not have to compute anything. One trap for anyone who revisits it: map(Rp,R) looks like the same map and returns b+1 for a, but only because a's normal form in R is already b+1, so it agrees by accident rather than by recording the correspondence. the suggestion was tested and the code declines it. pushForward1 is gone -- changes.m2:1827 records "'pushForward1(f,M)' has been replaced by 'relations coimage map(M,f)'" and the only survivals are commented-out doc at pushForward-doc.m2:95-121 -- and tu_canEmbed.m2:254-256 now reads ff1 = map(R,S,can1); G = map(coker F1,ff1); trim coimage G, giving betti {(0,{0},0)=>1, (1,{2},2)=>10}. not an M2 bug: a scratch C file exploring whether Python can be embedded in a C program, quoting William Stein on making Sage's 'from sage.all import *' avoid importing IPython so that 'sage -python' and 'sage -c' start faster. The question the exploration was for is settled affirmatively in M2 itself: d/python.d embeds CPython directly (Py_IsInitialized/Py_Initialize at :40), d/python-c.c is the conversion layer, and pythoncapi_compat.h tracks the modern C API. three asks: the third is met, the first two are one thing and are measured. Ask 3, an example of a dynamically loaded C library in a python module, is done well beyond the request -- installNumPyMethods with worked examples in Python/doc/numpy.m2 converting M2 matrices and vectors to NumPy arrays, plus a matplotlib tutorial with a rendered twisted-cubic.png; both are C extension modules in M2's embedded CPython. Asks 1 and 2 unmet: python.d:28 builds pythonObjectCell(po, hash_t(0)) with no registerFinalizer and no Py_DECREF, and the only three Py_DECREF calls in the interface (python-c.c:163,175,219) are on conversion temporaries. Measured two ways: sys.getrefcount on a list held in __main__ goes 2 -> 3 when M2 wraps it and stays 3 after the M2 reference is dropped and collectGarbage() and gc.collect() are both run; and 20 objects created in a loop with no M2 reference kept are all still alive afterwards. Caveat on the proof, since only the two together are conclusive: a refcount that stays put is also consistent with Boehm not having collected the cell, and that cannot be distinguished by observation precisely because there is no finalizer to watch fire. registerFinalizer exists as a MethodFunction, so the mechanism is available; the work is deciding per toExpr call site whether the reference is owned or borrowed, a wrong DECREF being worse than the leak, which is presumably why Dan wrote it as a task. Correcting an earlier claim of mine: Python.m2 has 14 TEST blocks, so the package is tested -- what is true is that none touches refcounts, lifetime or GC, and the three-line check above would be one. Searched issues and PRs: the interface has had a lot of work (#2130, #2302, #2316, #2523, #2605, #2631, #2639, #2692, #3025) and none is about reference counting

the same defect as #4515, which this catalog filed four days ago from 0-quotient-for-non-free-modules, and which leads with the well-definedness claim. Reproduces exactly, with an asymmetry #4515's example does not have: for f = inducedMap(R^1/x, R^1/x^2) and g = inducedMap(R^1/x, R^1/x^3) over ZZ/101[x], quotientRemainder(g,f) has isWellDefined first true while quotientRemainder(f,g) has it false. The mathematics agrees, which is why it is a good test case: quotientRemainder(f,g) wants q : R^1/x^2 -> R^1/x^3, and 1 sends x^2 to x^2, nonzero in R/x^3, whereas the other direction sends x^3 to 0 in R/x^2. Commented on #4515 with the pair and Dan's 2006 email asking 'Did I just not think about whether the resulting maps are well-defined?'

no longer reproduces: random(ZZ^2,ZZ^2,MaximalRank=>true) gives a different matrix every call, e.g. {3643,3321}/{206,3321} then {911,122}/{3121,335}. No fix commit identified, and the obvious candidate is wrong -- randomMR (genmat.m2, reached from :122) has had the randomizing blocks since it was written in 7fd73b1579 (2006-07-08), six months before this file (2007-01-05), so the identity output did not come from those being absent. For a square matrix the m>k and n>k branches are skipped and everything depends on the 'if m>1' and 'if n>1' row/column additions, whose coefficients are random(d0,R,opts) and random(d1,R,opts) with d0 = d1 = {} because degreeLength ZZ is 0. So the likeliest 2007 cause is random(List,Ring) returning 0 for that shape; it now returns varied values ({5,1,8,7,4}). Recorded as fixed on the observation rather than on an attributed commit

literally unmet -- randomHeight is still set up at actors5.d:1849, still calls rawSetRandomMax at :1931, and maxHeight is still the engine global (e/interface/random.cpp:17) -- but nothing observable rides on it, so eliminating it is internals work across the M2/engine boundary for no user-visible gain. Decisive point, from the maintainer: randomHeight is not exported. class randomHeight is Symbol at top level (it is setupvar'd into Core but absent from exports.m2), so it takes debug Core even to read. I had written this up as a bug on two leaks, and both are unobservable: mutablemat.m2:173 and :179 restore with 'randomHeight := s', colon-equals, which declares a local, so fillMatrix(m, Height => 100000) leaves the global at 100000; and genmat.m2:55-59 sets it and then errors between set and restore, so random(ZZ^2,ZZ^2,Height=>0) leaves it at 0. Neither is visible from the prompt -- with the global sitting at 100000, 400 samples of random(ZZ^1,ZZ^10) and 400 of random ZZ both stay within 10, because every consumer sets it from its own Height default before reading. So the two := are dead code rather than live bugs. On the same reading, changes.m2:2858 ('The variable randomHeight has been removed, replaced by [fillMatrix, Height] and [random, Height]') is accurate about the user surface, which is the only surface a release note is about -- I had first read it as a false claim. mutablemat.m2:171 and :177 both comment '-- silly global variable', so the file's opinion is shared. Adjacent tracker state: #2089 'Crash on random with Height => 0' is open but no longer crashes, erroring cleanly at genmat.m2:56 ('expected a positive height'); #999 'random QQ' is the other open one

Mike's suggestion was taken, five weeks after he made it. His email is dated 2009-06-16 and the file was created the same day (bd88e96c0c); b8246778dd (2009-07-20) 'add operator ..<' added it. does not reproduce, with the caveat that the file says the corruption happened only 'sometimes!'. Ran Anton's transcript five times -- M2 as 'openInOut openListener "$:PORT"', a python client sending 'hi there', a 60-character buffer string held across the read -- and the buffer was byte-identical afterwards every time; the file's diagnostic, substring(buffer,0,#newstring) == newstring, is false, where in the bug it was true because the read had overwritten the buffer's head. Five trials is weak evidence against an intermittent memory bug, so this is 'no longer observed' rather than a proven fix, and no fix commit is identifiable. What makes it plausible is the era: the D-language string and buffer handling was rewritten for C++ in fc4f09790b (2011-12-27, 'refactor scc -> C++ ... for safety'), long after the 2006 report. Worth re-testing if anyone sees string corruption around sockets again

fixed, and the tracker carries the same report twice. Reproducing it needs read to be genuinely blocked, so a pipe that supplies input immediately does not exercise it -- driven from python with a six-second gap, alarm fires while read waits. Then: 'error: failed to read file : interrupted' followed by a normal numbered prompt, where the file's transcript shows the '>> ' prompt persisting through the next two inputs (o9, o10). c2bb79553a (2020-05-15, #1161 'Fix prompt overriding when read is interrupted') closed #1160, the same complaint from a user; d5fe98839a (2023-10-04, 'fix read() #2951', in #2991) closed #2951 'missing prompt after read()', a later relapse. #1159, "'read' doesn't recover after interrupt", is the third and also closed

the premise expired with the platform. The file is about macOS shipping libedit's readline shim, which provides completion_matches but not rl_completion_matches or _rl_comment_begin, so M2 had to compile its own readline; macOS builds now get real GNU readline from Homebrew. Half the ask was done regardless: 37c060e7d4 (2015-06-11) 'a less stringent test for libreadline' deleted the hand-written link test 'extern int rl_set_prompt(); extern int _rl_comment_begin; int main () { return rl_set_prompt() + _rl_comment_begin; }' in favour of AC_SEARCH_LIBS(rl_set_prompt,readline,,BUILD_readline=yes). The other symbol survives and is genuinely used, not just tested -- configure.ac:1227 checks rl_completion_matches and M2lib.c:130 calls it -- so avoiding it would mean changing the source too. And the tree moved the other way: c27ce84b40 (2018-06-25) added a fourth reason to bundle, 'build libreadline if the existing one does not define rl_catch_signals', so BUILD_readline is now a deliberate fallback from four checks rather than an accident of two over-strict ones. #726 (closed) and #4321 (open, cmake syslibroot on macosx) are the nearest tracker items and neither is this

duplicate of #708 'floating point weirdness', open since 2017 and worked on by the maintainer, whose own body closes with toExternalString oo -> .9007199254740991p53e16, the same function this file shows. State today: the transcript's trailing e0 is gone (toExternalString .3 is .29999999999999999p53) and the value round-trips, but seventeen significant digits are emitted where one would do, since value ".3p53" == .3. Not a blanket policy -- .5 and .25 print as .5p53 and .25p53 because those decimals are exact in binary, and 1. prints .1p53e1 -- so M2 prints short when it can be exact and otherwise falls back to full precision. The maintainer's comment of 2024-11-03 states the mechanism and the obstacle: 'using mpfr_get_str, we get the mathematically closest option. But for readability, we probably want the option with the fewest number of digits. There are various algorithms for this (Dragon4, Grisu3, Ryu), but as far as I can tell, they haven't been implemented for MPFR yet.' #3477 bumped p53 digits from 15 to 16 and that comment notes 17 is required, which matches the 17 measured here; #1579 is collateral. Commented with the one thing the row adds, that the symptom shows on an ordinary number rather than only near 2^53. Search note: the cache found nothing because the decisive text is in a comment and bin/fetch-issues does not cache comments, and #708's title shares no vocabulary with this row -- gh search issues, which does index comments, found it on the term 'ryu'

nothing in this repository to change. The file opens 'for the web site' and asks for two literature searches -- Google Scholar and MathSciNet, both for references to 'macaulay2, a software system' -- plus code to dedupe the combined list. That is neither a defect nor a feature of Macaulay2 and has no closing condition an issue in this tracker could carry; the artifact would live on the web site, which is not this tree. PackageCitations.m2 exists but points the other way, generating citations for packages rather than collecting papers that cite M2, and #586 ('support cite command for packages') and #864 ('fix cite command') are that lineage. Searched the cache and gh search issues, which indexes comments, for google scholar, MathSciNet, citations and bibliography: nothing about collecting citations of M2. Not recorded as obsolete because that would assert something about what the web site publishes today, which was not checked

unmet in every particular, and cheaper now than when it was written. regularity is declared at betti.m2:244 with Options => {Weights => null} only -- no Strategy, no Algorithm, no addHook or runHooks anywhere for it -- and the real methods live in Complexes/ChainComplex.m2:640-654, where regularity Ideal, Module and Complex all go through betti(freeResolution ...) with no dispatch point. The package the file names exists, packages/Regularity.m2, but exports mRegularity, CM, MonCurve (:22): a parallel function, so a user who writes regularity I cannot reach its algorithm, and the package's own tests assert the two agree by hand, 'assert(mRegularity(I, MonCurve => true) == regularity I)'. The consequence is still accumulating: #4191, an open PR, adds weightedRegularity to Depth.m2 as a third name for a related computation. What has changed in the file's favour is that hookified methods are now M2's conventional pattern -- freeResolution, pushForward, minimalPrimes and kernel all dispatch this way -- so the mechanism is standard rather than novel, and the file's second clause, 'the value of Strategy should be checked, somehow', is what runHooks provides. #3321 (closed) is regularity over quotient rings, unrelated. Searched cache and gh search issues; nothing on hookifying regularity

the proposed model is dead and the need is met several times over. Reinteract (fishsoup.net/software/reinteract, Owen Taylor) has had no release since around 2010. What the file wanted from it -- tab completion, tooltips with information about what is on screen, inline graphs, portable to Windows and Mac -- is what the Jupyter notebook interface provides, and #605 'Jupyter interface' was closed 2025-10-02; Jupyter is a symbol in Core (changes.m2:1246). The wiki carries Using-Macaulay2-with-Jupyter, -with-VSCode, -with-Sublime, -with-Org-Mode and -with-Emacs pages plus Interfaces-to-Macaulay2, so there are now several, and Macaulay2Web is a browser front end besides. #675 (vim) is the other closed interface issue

both halves met, measured against the file's own numbers. It complains that replacing 80100 times in a 5643739-byte cedict is 'too slow, compared to emacs'; on a corpus of the same shape and size (5286599 bytes, 80100 lines, all 80100 substitutions firing -- output grew 881100 bytes) the file's own pattern runs in 0.246 s, against sed -E at 0.26 s and python3 re.sub at 0.214 s on the same file. #1425 'Switch to Boost::regex' (390894fe9f, 2020-07-26) is the change. 'Also, make it interruptable' is met too: alarm 1 during a 2.1-second replace over a 42 MB corpus interrupts it. Boost adds a bound of its own -- a catastrophic pattern like (a+)+b raises 'The complexity of matching the regular expression exceeded predefined bounds ... to prevent eternal matches' -- so a runaway match cannot happen either. #3513 and #332 are the live replace issues, about linear algebra speed and unicode

reproduces, and the finding is broader than the file's. Finding the ring shape took three tries: the file's F() returns a plain quotient coefficient ring, since with GF or toField the coefficient generator is not reachable at all and R_2 is 'index 2 out of bounds 0 .. 1'. With zzF = () -> (k0 := ZZ/2[ww]; k0/(k0_0^2+k0_0+1)), R = zzF()[x,y] and S = zzF()[x,y]: R_2 and S_2 are both ww, I = ideal(x+ww), and sub(I, {R_2 => S_2}) errors. The message has changed since 2009 -- 'expected substitution values and omitted generators to be in compatible rings' where the file has 'expected ww to be a generator of R' -- and it is not specific to the coefficient generator: sub(I, {R_0 => S_0}) fails identically, while (map(S,R)) I returns ideal(x+ww). So any partial substitution between two separately-constructed but identical rings fails, and the full ring map shows the answer is computable. The error is arguably honest, since with y omitted the result's ring is ambiguous between R and S, but the same shape is accepted when R and S are the same ring, which makes the failure look incidental. Searched cache and gh search issues: #1224 is QQ[a,a,a], replicated names within one ring; #1011 is a doc request that M2 does not enforce well-definedness; #1183 is GaloisField coefficient rings, the shape that here errors on R_2 instead. The maintainer's unpushed PR_ring-maps work is about which conversions are canonical, a different axis

three asks. The identity predicate is met: RingMap == ZZ at ringmap.m2:30-32, where f == 1 is 'source f === target f and f === id_(source f)'. The dispatch ask is unmet and is the same missed predicate as #4579, filed from this catalog out of 1-flattenRing-can-save-time, whose second half is that applying a ring map never short-circuits when f == 1 -- here it is composing rather than applying. RingMap * RingMap (ringmap.m2:383-397) unconditionally computes g matrix f, builds a fresh rawRingMap and constructs a new RingMap; over QQ[a..h], 200 compositions take 0.021s for f*zzid and 0.0205s for zzid*f against 0.035s for f*f, so cheaper but not free. Probe trap worth keeping: === on RingMaps is structural, so f*zzid === f is true and f.RawRingMap === g.RawRingMap is true, and neither shows a short-circuit -- what does is a marker in the cache, f.cache#"zzmarker" = 1 being invisible from (f*zzid).cache, proving a distinct object. The third ask, Schubert2 doing all pullbacks by ring maps to optimise composition on cycle classes, depends on the composition short-circuit existing first and is a package refactor. Commented on #4579 with the composition timings and the === trap. #1919 (RingMap.cache.DegreeMap) and #1518 (kernels over ZZ) are the other open RingMap items, neither this

the premise is gone: M2 no longer builds rpms, so there is no *.spec file whose %dir entries could be missing. beeb464469 (2025-09-13) removed the --enable-rpm configure option and 6c833cbf0c (2025-09-08) the Debian packaging directory, both by the maintainer who now packages M2 downstream; M2/distributions/ holds only freebsd, install, tar and top. The report itself is a 2008 email from a Warwick user about RedHat rpms on Dan's own download site leaving empty directory trees behind after removal, and Dan's guess that not listing directory names in the spec file explained it. Same seam as 1-porting, 1-opensuse-build-service and 1-rpm-repository. #60, #240 and #678 are the surviving rpm issues, all closed and all about building rather than about spec-file directory ownership

same seam as its sibling 1-rpm-directories-linger, and dead for the same reason: M2 stopped shipping rpms (beeb464469 removed --enable-rpm, 2025-09-13), so there is no set of rpms for createrepo to index. The file is six lines noting that createrepo had moved from linux.duke.edu to createrepo.baseurl.org and recording the invocation; createrepo itself was superseded by createrepo_c years ago. Distribution repositories for M2 are now the distributions' own concern, which is the arrangement #4528 from this catalog serves by making configure report what it found for packagers

the need was met by a better mechanism than the one proposed. The file wants examples run by forking a warm process and redirecting i/o, for which it says M2 would need close ZZ, open String and dup2(ZZ,ZZ) -- none of which exists. Instead M2 grew capture (examples.m2:59-62, capture = method(Options => {UserMode => true, PackageExports => null}) over the built-in capture'), which runs an example in the *current* process with output collected, so there is no fork, no file-descriptor juggling and no startup cost at all -- strictly better than the proposal for the purpose stated. It is the default path: captureTestResult calls isCapturable and prefers capturing, falling back to a subprocess only when the example is not capturable (examples.m2:147 lists the exclusions, e.g. anything matching temporaryFileName). No single fix commit is identifiable; capture predates 2008 in some form and the method wrapper is later

unmet, and the remedy has become less applicable rather than more. Nothing in examples.m2 or testing.m2 sets up an unwritable directory -- no chmod, no fileMode -- so a package that writes stray files into the current directory still does so unnoticed. But capture (examples.m2:59-62), which is now the default path for running examples and which settled the sibling row 1-running-examples, runs them in M2's own process, so there is no per-example working directory whose permissions could be changed; doing it to M2's cwd would affect the whole run. M2 already has a blunter form of the idea in the --read-only-files command-line option, which refuses output files globally (stdio.d). The concern is real and acknowledged in passing: examples.m2:147 excludes from capture anything matching temporaryFileName, commented 'this is sometimes bug prone', so examples that make files are already a special case, by exclusion rather than prevention. If revisited, the plausible shape today is running check with cwd set somewhere disposable and diffing it afterwards, rather than an unwritable directory. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues; #1217 'Running M2 as root' is the only permissions-adjacent open item

does exactly what the file proposes. For R = QQ[x], S = R[y], f = map(R^2,R^2,matrix{{x,0},{0,1}}) and b = y_S, b*f returns a matrix over S with target and source S^2, and target(b*f) == S ** target f is true; entries are {{x*y,0},{0,y}}, so the R-entries are promoted and scaled. The mechanism is toSameRing (matrix.m2:13-21), called by RingElement * Matrix at :98-100, which promotes whichever side is promotable into the other's ring via isPromotable and errors otherwise. The file's condition that the modules be free is not needed for this to work. 0a494d5f6e (2009-01-24) is where toSameRing appears, its message including 'improve tensor product coercion', and 7a3be96374 and c969a5299c (2024) extended promotion for tensor products; the file is undated in the tree but the google-group exchange it cites puts it around then. #3906 'Constant times matrix fail' is the closed tracker version of the same area

unmet as asked, and the need has a shorter spelling than the proposal. Both transcripts still error identically: scan(5,9,identity) and apply(5,9,identity) give 'expected argument 1 to be a list or sequence'. But apply(5..8, identity) is (5,6,7,8), and .. is how ranges are written throughout M2 -- including the ..< operator this catalog settled as fixed in the previous batch, added at Mike's request in b8246778dd. The overload also carries a real cost: apply(5,f) iterates 0..4, so the first argument would mean 'count' at arity two and 'start' at arity three. The live requests in this family are about what the function may do rather than how the range is given -- #3870 'apply/scan should accept continue' and #4184 'try modifier in apply,select,etc', both open -- and nothing has asked for the two-integer form in seventeen years. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues

the shebang works. Wrote the file's own two lines -- '#! /usr/bin/M2 --script' then 'print a' -- made it executable and ran it: it executes, and scriptCommandLine is {./foo}. The file's transcript instead shows M2 failing to find ./foo, looking for it in the d/ source directory, which is what a build-tree M2 with an unset prefix would do. Handling is at startup.m2.in:534-546: commandLine#1 == "--script" takes commandLine#2 as the file and puts the rest in scriptCommandLine, with :464 erroring if --script is not first, which is what a shebang guarantees. No fix commit identified -- the failure looks like a 1.2-era build-tree path problem rather than a defect in the option. #234 'M2 --script' is open and about the option's design, not this

the system the file says is needed exists. about (help.m2:658, options {Body => false}) searches the installed documentation databases and returns numbered hits across all packages -- about "kernel" lists nodes from Complexes, CpMackeyFunctors and so on -- with Body => true to search node text rather than just keys; apropos (help.m2:639) matches symbol names; help and viewHelp do direct lookup. #774 'master documentation index and search function' is closed and is the tracker's version of this same request. The second sentence, 'Boolean operators in search expressions would be good, too', is half-served rather than met: about takes a regular expression, so alternation gives OR (about "kernel|cokernel"), while AND has no spelling and would need filtering two searches. Left unfiled because the live requests in this area already point at improving search rather than providing it -- #4324 'apropos with fuzzy search' and #4509 'Documentation nodes should be able to declare search aliases', the latter filed from this catalog out of 0-doc-Keywords, whose note records a single term returning 131 hits, which is the case where AND would actually help

select is a method function and users can add methods to it, which is the whole ask. class select is MethodFunctionWithOptions with eleven methods installed: (select,Thing,Function), (select,BasicList,Function), (select,BasicList,Type), (select,HashTable,Function), (select,Set,Function), (select,String,String), (select,String,String,String), (select,ZZ,Function), (select,ZZ,BasicList,Function), (select,ZZ,HashTable,Function), (select,ZZ,Set,Function). 3dc3352f44 (2020-07-28, #1425) 'allow select to have options, so the regex parameters can be adjusted' is the commit that gave it options; it was already a method by then. #578 and #579, both closed, are about what select means on Sets and HashTables rather than about its dispatch

the useful third of the file was taken into Core; the package it asks for was not, and nothing has asked for one since. recipN at hilbert.m2:12-26 is the file's recip1 verbatim, comments word for word ('n is a positive integer', 'g always has the form 1 plus terms weight 1,2,...,m-1', '1-f*g always has terms of wt m and higher'), sitting under '-- Local utilities', declared with := so file-local, beside a truncatePower helper and used by the Hilbert series machinery at :42 -- so the algorithm runs on every hilbertSeries call but only as private plumbing for that one caller. recip2 (constant unit) and recip (unit times an invertible monomial, using weightRange and exponents for the Laurent case) have no counterpart, and those are precisely the general cases a series package would need. No such package exists; PlaneCurveLinearSeries, SymbolicPowers and QthPower are unrelated. Not filed because a 'write a package' issue with no consumer sits indefinitely -- the README records that shape as why the wishlist files survived twenty-five years -- and the two open series issues would not be closed by it: #974 'Can't take value of a Hilbert series' and #598 'Defect in differentiation of Laurent series' each want a specific fix. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues for series expansion, power series, recipN, truncatePower

the ask is unmet but the need is met, via debug Core, which the maintainer pointed out. setRandomSeed returns the NEW seed, not the previous one, because system.m2:146-148 ends with the assignment 'randomSeed = seed' (commented 'magic assignment, calls rawSetRandomSeed internally'), and randomSeed is not exported -- class randomSeed at top level is Symbol and it is absent from exports.m2. But debug Core is the supported route to private symbols and the round trip works: old = randomSeed (117061313407862), setRandomSeed 12345, setRandomSeed old, back to 117061313407862. It is also less private than the export status suggests, since setRandomSeed-doc.m2:17 names it -- 'Otherwise sets randomSeed to a value based on seed' -- so a reader is told the variable exists, though it has no node of its own. Core does the same save/restore internally with pushvar(symbol randomSeed, ...) and popvar at examples.m2:75 and :122. What remains is ergonomics: debug Core puts Core's whole private dictionary on dictionaryPath to read one integer, with the shadowing costs several rows in this catalog are about -- a cost of debug Core generally rather than of this feature. Changing setRandomSeed's return value would also break callers relying on the present one. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues for setRandomSeed, randomSeed, previous seed, restore seed: #89, #3800, #978, all closed and about randomness in tests

a latent hazard in Core-private code, with the file's own instance gone and no reachable case found. buildPrefix, which the file calls 'exactly the situation', is no longer anywhere in m2/. The mechanism it wished for -- 'Dynamic scoping, as in lisp, has its uses!' -- was built as pushvar/popvar (Core.m2:67-73) and is used at eight sites: inDebugger (code.m2:282), randomSeed and OutputDictionary (examples.m2:75,86), printWidth (format.m2:317 and installPackage.m2:381), currentPackage (installPackage.m2:696), flagInhomogeneity (modules2.m2:136). It does not address the hazard: pushvar(symbol randomSeed, 999) followed by an error leaves randomSeed at 999 and the varstack unbalanced, restored only by an explicit popvar. Core.m2:65 already says '-- TODO: move to the interpreter and make thread-safe'. Not filed because no user-visible instance could be constructed: the most promising live site, installPackage.m2:381 pushing printWidth with two deliberate error calls defined just above it, cannot be reached -- forcing one of those errors with a doc node named "Top" fires at document.m2:699 during package load, before the pushvar, and printWidth came back unchanged at 55. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues for pushvar, popvar and state-after-interrupt: nothing; #1098 (closed) is about restoring the terminal on SIGSEGV

the effect behind the ask is already delivered, and the residue is cosmetic. setup() (files.m2:488-508) does run unconditionally -- supplantStringFile for ~/.profile-Macaulay2 and ~/.login-Macaulay2, then mungeFile into ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile or ~/.zprofile, with nothing consulting PATH first -- but the snippet it writes is idempotent: bashtempl (files.m2:405-418) prepends a directory only when the variable does not already contain it, and setup-doc.m2 documents exactly that, 'add the appropriate directory to the front of the environment variable PATH ... unless that directory already occurs in the path'. So no duplicate PATH entry results; what the file objects to is only that the init files get edited when there was nothing new to add. Correcting an earlier claim of mine, that nothing checks PATH: nothing in setup() does, but the written snippet does. The maintainer raised the larger question of whether setup() is obsolete. Evidence against: it is referenced from ov_getting_started.m2:231, ov_editors_emacs.m2:92 and distributions/top/INSTALL.in:80 (which runs ./M2 -e 'setup();exit 0'), and users were hitting it recently enough to file #1061, #1138, #1139, #1460 (all closed 2019-2020) and #1068 (open), with real fixes in 480e0899a4 and 4a66fd9023. Evidence for: its audience is now only people installing from the binary tarball into a private location, since packaged installs put M2 on PATH, and the doc's Caveat is about multi-architecture shared home directories, the same dead scenario that settled 1-profile-init. Retiring setup() would mean deciding those three sets of instructions together, which is larger than this row

a question rather than a request -- 'should we do something like this?' over IPython's first-run banner -- and the answer is no, for reasons the pasted banner itself supplies. Its distinctive feature is 'Please press <RETURN> to start IPython', a blocking prompt, which is incompatible with the non-interactive uses that now dominate: M2 --script, capture, example generation and CI. IPython abandoned that banner years ago, so the model is gone too. The underlying behaviour is unchanged: setUpApplicationDirectory (called from packages.m2:331) creates ~/.Macaulay2 with init.m2, code/, local/, an index.html and a README on first run, silently -- observed directly while testing Configuration under a redirected HOME two batches ago, where a fresh home acquired the whole tree and the only output came from the package's own Configuration. The need is served more quietly by that README: a user who looks finds an explanation. A non-blocking one-line notice would be the defensible version, but first-run output is exactly what breaks reproducible example output across the ~8500 .out files, and nobody has asked in seventeen years. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues for first-run banners, applicationDirectory and welcome messages: nothing; #2861 is a package update announcement

the mechanism was declined with a reason and the need met another way, both recorded in the source. files.m2:445-450 has the exec-path fix commented out with the explanation beside it: '-- the exec-path fix is not needed, because we exec the shell and ask it to find M2'. What is in emacsfixes instead is ('PATH', currentLayout#"bin", emacsenvtempl), so ~/.emacs-Macaulay2 sets the PATH environment variable, which is what lets emacs's shell find M2 -- the need in the file's one sentence. #67 '.emacs-Maculay2 may also need to set PATH variable' is the tracker's version of the same point and is closed, consistent with PATH now being set. So this is fixed rather than wontfix: the ask names exec-path, the need is that M2 be findable from emacs, and it is

both complaints are gone. The self-shadowing warning in the transcript -- 'symbol fourierMotzkin in FourierMotzkin.Dictionary is shadowed by a symbol in FourierMotzkin.Dictionary', a package shadowing itself, with a fourierMotzkin$0 synonym invented for it -- does not occur. Reproducing it needs a package that is not preloaded, since loadPackage "FourierMotzkin" now refuses with 'package FourierMotzkin not reloaded; try Reload => true'; with Posets and loadPackage(..., LoadDocumentation => true, Reload => true) the only output is ' -- warning: reloading Posets; recreate instances of types from this package', which is the informative warning added by #3852 and credited in this catalog on 1-loadPackage. The second complaint, 'also, the tests didn't run' (check printing nothing in the transcript), is also gone -- check works, as this catalog established on 1-check-inputs where check(0, "Posets") runs 36 tests. #1184 'New notation for shadowed symbols' and #4292 'Stray symbols from packages' are the live open items in this area and neither is this

the ask was granted, and in the shape the file guessed it would be. (sheaf, Ideal) and (sheaf, Variety, Ideal) are both installed -- twelve sheaf methods in all -- and sheaf I for a graded ideal returns a CoherentSheaf. So the file's own reservation was accepted rather than resolved: 'the result should be a sheaf of ideals, not a sheaf of modules; and it seems sort of silly to invent the whole class of sheaves of ideals just so sheaf I will do something. But, why not?' -- no such class was invented, and the result is a sheaf of modules. That is the answer to 'why not', arrived at by doing the cheap half

a ratio with no target, and the maintainer's question -- gcd of what? -- is the right one, since the file benchmarks only QQ[a,b]. Measured across rings with operands built outside the timing loop: QQ[a,b] gcd 18.7 us against multiply 3.02 us (6.2x), QQ[t] 19.9 vs 3.12 (6.4x), ZZ/32003[a,b] 14.1 vs 2.19 (6.4x), ZZ 3.0 vs 0.37 (8.2x). So the ratio is uniform rather than specific to the case measured, and it has roughly halved since the file was written (11.7 reported, ~6 now) with nobody aiming at it. What the spread does show is that the cost is overhead rather than algorithm: any polynomial gcd is 14-20 us however trivial, gcd of two 200-digit integers is 4.1 us against 3.0 us for gcd(12,18), and real work scales sensibly -- gcd((a+b)^12,(a-b)^12) is 86 us and a pair sharing a degree-12 factor is 230 us. Not filed because there is no stated criterion for success and no profile establishing the overhead is avoidable; the likely answer, conversion to and from Factory, is architectural. One harness correction worth recording: a first pass showed QQ[t] at 36.7 us, apparently slower with one variable than two, because t+1 was being constructed inside the timed loop -- the anomaly was mine. #321 and #1851 are closed; the one open gcd issue, #4583 from this catalog, is about correctness

two of three clauses unmet, and the measurements are worse than the file's. Interruptability is met: alarm 2 during a 45-second sort interrupts it. The speed clause is not: sorting 50000 equal elements takes 19.96 s against the file's target of .01 s, and pre-sorted distinct input is worse still at 45.73 s, where the same 50000 values shuffled sort in .061 s -- a factor of 750. Quadratic, established by scaling rather than one point: pre-sorted 10000 takes 1.79 s, 20000 takes 7.22 s (4.0x for 2x the data) and 40000 takes 35.7 s (4.9x). Duplication scales the same way: random from 0..99 is .447 s, all-equal is 19.96 s. internalsort is a recursive quicksort at actors3.d:477-509 (sortfun -> basicsort2, setupfun at :535); the pivot is already randomized, 'a := randomint() % b' at :479, which is why random input is fast and why the pre-sorted collapse is surprising -- the naive diagnosis is wrong. A per-call linear shift runs after both recursive calls, 'for k from l+1 to j do sortlist.(k-1) = sortlist.k', which is worth examining, but I did not establish it as the cause and the issue says so. The third clause, tallying duplicates first, would address the 19.96 s case and not the 45.73 s one. List construction was excluded from the timings (toList(0..49999) is .008 s). Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues: #101 and #650 are open and about sort's semantics, not its speed; nothing on complexity

sort accepts a function: sort({3,1,2}, x -> -x) returns {3,2,1}. The tracker's version, #1154 'feature request: sort accept order function', is closed. Worth recording the semantics, since the file asks for a 'comparison function' and what exists is a key function -- the second argument is applied to each element and the results compared, which is why x -> -x sorts descending rather than being read as a two-argument comparator. That covers the common case and composes with inversePermutation and the rest, and a genuine comparator would be a different signature. #4529, 'sort(List) advertises DegreeOrder and MonomialOrder, which it ignores', is closed and was filed from this catalog

a tentative suggestion -- 'Maybe we should turn on this option in the debug mode' -- superseded from both ends. configure.ac carries no -fstack-protector, no _FORTIFY_SOURCE and no hardening flags at all, so it is literally unmet. But release builds get hardened by whoever packages M2: Debian and Ubuntu apply -fstack-protector-strong and -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 through dpkg-buildflags and Fedora through its macros, and GCC on those distributions defaults to -fstack-protector-strong anyway -- which matters more since M2 stopped shipping its own packaging (beeb464469, 6c833cbf0c), so the builds users install are not M2's. And the debug case the file actually names is better served by the sanitizer builds the tree supports: AddressSanitizer catches the same buf[101]=12 and reports the offending write with a location, where -fstack-protector only notices a smashed canary at function return and aborts. unmet and not worth the cost. Triple quotes are not a delimiter: zzs = """abc""" gives 'no method for adjacent objects: "abc" (of class String) SPACE "" (of class String)', so it parses as three juxtaposed strings, an empty one either side of a normal one, and /// remains the only verbatim form. The file proposes replacing /// rather than adding an alternative, and /// is load-bearing across Macaulay2Doc and every package that writes documentation, including the doc ///...///  idiom itself, so a replacement is a breaking change across the ecosystem for a syntax preference borrowed from Python. Adding """ alongside would not be free either: "" is a valid empty string and adjacent juxtaposition already gives """" a meaning, so the grammar interaction needs resolving rather than just admitting the token. Nothing in seventeen years has asked. a request for a computer-algebra layer M2 does not have, recorded as one user's wish in two lines with no defect and no specification. What exists is an Expression hierarchy -- Sum, Product, Power, Divide, BinaryOperation, Holder, with hold to build one and expressionValue to evaluate it -- but it exists to render mathematics, being what net, describe and texMath are built on, not to manipulate it: expand is an unbound symbol, expressionValue is Core-private, and nothing simplifies, collects terms or substitutes into an unevaluated expression. M2's answer to symbolic expansion and substitution is to work in an actual ring, where QQ[x,y] gives both with real semantics; the cases that do not fit a ring are exactly the ones a CAS handles and M2 does not. 'Expansion, substitution, etc.' is a project without a boundary, so an issue would have no closing condition. Searched cache, PRs and gh search issues for symbolic algebra, computer algebra, expand and symbolic manipulation: nothing. The adjacent items are #1754, 'Wishlist: Make Expressions work with inequalities', and #4595, filed from this catalog today for not Expression -- both adding operators to Expression, a long way short of a manipulation layer
